newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs adjust privatisation law.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs adjust privatisation law.

text.p: Bosnian Serb politicians have adopted some of the amendments suggested by foreign experts to get their fledgling privatisation programme on track in Serb-controlled territory, a Serb official said on Wednesday.
Bosnia's two entities -- the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic -- prepared separate privatisation laws shortly after fighting ended in November 1995.
But foreign economic experts criticised the Serb model because up to 55 percent of state assets were transferred to state-controlled "socially oriented funds".
Slavisa Rakovic, Bosnian Serb economic adviser, said parliament had adopted amendments on Monday which placed limits on state investment funds.
The funds would be allowed to obtain a maximum 47 percent stake in a company and future legislation could set stricter limits, Rakovic told Reuters.
"The role of the funds will be determined through a new law on funds, which can be expected to further reduce the state-controlled funds," he said.
World Bank experts had proposed a number of changes to the Serb privatisation legislation to make the laws more effective and transparent.
"The original version of the law was something we thought could be improved significantly," said one World Bank official, who asked not to be named.
The Serb legislation calls for privatisation of state-owned companies but excludes strategic sectors and infrastructure, according to a World Bank report.

The amendments passed this week increase the ownership stake available to the public from 30 to 38 percent and call for a lottery system to distribute shares instead of a voucher system, Rakovic said.
The law still only allows private investors a 15 percent share in state-owned companies, a provision which the World Bank has criticised as too low.
Even with the amendments adopted this week, the privatisation law will have to be revisited by the Serb assembly, the World Bank official said.
"It will have to make the notion of privatisation and private ownership much clearer," he said. "In fact, the role of the funds could be reduced to below 30 percent."
The Serbs are eager to press ahead with the privatisation process to help revive their shattered economy.
But growth there lags far behind that in the Moslem-Croat federation.

The international community has committed more than one billion dollars to the country for peacetime reconstruction since 1996 but the Serb entity has received only two percent of the money because Serb leaders failed to comply with provisions of the peace treaty.
Their former enemies in the federation enjoy an annual economic growth rate of 50 percent and analysts expect growth to continue at 35 percent for the next three years.
But the Moslem-Croat federation parliament has yet to adopt the draft privatisation laws which were sent to the parliament last November because of political deadlock over other issues.
